parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sampling period `Ts = 0.2` s specified in TASK.md; fixed because the samples have a known time spacing.

parameters.name: gf
parameters.description: Gain of `v_f`, jointly estimated by 5-second rollout least squares.

parameters.name: ga
parameters.description: Gain of `v_a`, jointly estimated by the same rollout least squares.

estimation.criterion: Minimize the sum of squared open-loop rollout residuals in `x` (m), `y` (m), and heading (rad), over 25 transitions (5 s) per fitting window. The heading residual is the principal circular difference multiplied by a fixed conversion of 0.25 m/rad before squaring. This joint criterion constrains turning as well as translation, avoiding the weak angular identifiability of an `x`-only objective in some orientations. The conversion is an analyst-chosen balance, comparable to the distance traveled over a few seconds, not an estimated sensor-noise variance. No later logged pose corrects a rollout.
estimation.data: `data/train.csv`, all three trajectories (`trajectory = 1`, `trajectory = 2`, and `trajectory = 3`), treated as separate experiments. Fit windows start at within-trajectory zero-based rows `0, 5, ..., 120`; each uses the logged initial pose and the next 25 transitions (5 s), without later state correction. Thus 75 windows use inputs through row 144 and target states through row 145. The last four samples are not direct fitting targets because no complete 25-transition window starting on their command-block grid ends there. They are included in the sliding-window validation (starts at every available row through row 124) and in full-trajectory diagnostics. Block-aligned fitting starts reflect the one-second command schedule and reduce near-duplicate starts. No transition crosses trajectory boundaries.
estimation.method: Bounded nonlinear least squares using `scipy.optimize.least_squares`, its default trust-region reflective method, two-point finite-difference Jacobian, linear loss, `ftol = 1e-10`, `xtol = 1e-10`, `gtol = 1e-10`, and `max_nfev = 400`. This directly optimizes the required multi-step simulation rather than differentiating noisy logged poses or minimizing only one-step increments. All final fitted parameters are estimated together in this one rollout-fitting step. The calculation is deterministic and uses no random seed. Starting values were `gf = 0.83` and `ga = 0.68`, rounded from preliminary steady-command regressions on the training data. Bounds were `0.2 <= gf <= 1.5` and `0.1 <= ga <= 1.5`, broad positive gain bounds chosen to avoid implausible reversed command response.

discussion.family: Discrete-time unicycle/differential-drive kinematics with calibrated command response. A general reference for unicycle kinematics is Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani and Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control (Springer, 2009), cited from memory without consulting the book during this round. The supplied task, rather than that reference, defines the robot and sampling period. The translation uses the explicit midpoint (second-order Runge-Kutta) direction for a constant command within a sample.
discussion.interpretation: `x`, `y`, and `phi` are the current planar pose, `v_f` and `v_a` are the current forward and angular commands, and `Ts` is the fixed sampling period. `gf` converts commanded forward speed to effective logged forward speed, and `ga` calibrates angular command response. Translation adds a body-forward increment projected onto the world axes. The heading update uses `atan2(sin(phi + Ts*(ga*v_a)), cos(phi + Ts*(ga*v_a)))` to wrap the angle; wrapping does not alter either translation projection. `gf*v_f` is effective forward speed and `ga*v_a` is effective angular speed. The midpoint direction is `phi + 0.5*Ts*ga*v_a`. There is no assumed drift at zero command and no spatially varying coefficient. The complete state-update expressions are `x + Ts*(gf*v_f)*cos(phi + 0.5*Ts*(ga*v_a))`, `y + Ts*(gf*v_f)*sin(phi + 0.5*Ts*(ga*v_a))`, and `atan2(sin(phi + Ts*(ga*v_a)), cos(phi + Ts*(ga*v_a)))`.
discussion.origin: The pose projections `cos(phi)` and `sin(phi)` and additive heading dynamics come from differential-drive physical reasoning. I tested Euler, midpoint and exact constant-command arc integration. I retained only midpoint in the pool because their 5-second validation errors were almost identical and they are the same structural family. `gf*v_f` and `ga*v_a` were the simplest calibrations consistent with the observed reduced speeds. The fixed half-step direction `phi + 0.5*Ts*ga*v_a` follows numerical integration, not symbolic search.
discussion.limitations: Constant gains average the command-response nonlinearities and trajectory-dependent changes visible in the training data. Midpoint translation omits the exact arc chord factor, negligible for the observed per-sample turn angles. On all training sliding windows, `x` rollout RMSE is 0.030027 m; equal-trajectory pooled leave-one-trajectory-out `x` RMSE is 0.029936 m, computed on 25-transition (5 s) windows with one-sample start spacing. These results are diagnostics, not test scores. Only positive forward commands were observed: `0.000034 <= v_f <= 0.298156` m/s, and angular commands satisfy `-0.948148 <= v_a <= 0.941161` rad/s (rounded extrema of `data/train.csv`). Reverse motion and larger commands are not validated. The logs cannot separate true actuator response from odometry distortion. Command-change residuals show lag and within-block correlation, but the allowed state has neither actuator velocity nor previous commands, so this memoryless model cannot reproduce that lag exactly. Long rollouts accumulate error; 30-second training diagnostics are not evidence of 5-second test accuracy. Validation uses only three held-out training trajectories, with overlapping windows; it is not an independent test set and gives no reliable confidence interval.
